title: Almost Everyone Thinks They’re on the Right Road… Until Jesus Says Otherwise
paragraphs:
Almost Everyone Thinks They’re on the Right Road… Until Jesus Says Otherwise
The Startling Reality Behind “Wide Is the Gate That Leads to Destruction” — And Why This May Be the Most Important Warning You Ever Read
There are verses in Scripture that comfort us.
There are verses that strengthen us.
Then there are verses that stop us in our tracks.

Jesus spoke one of those warnings in what we now call the Sermon on the Mount—not to pagans, not to atheists, not to people who had never heard of God, but to crowds who believed they were seeking Him.
His words were startling then.
They are even more unsettling now.

"Enter through the narrow gate. For wide is the gate and broad is the road that leads to destruction, and many enter through it. But small is the gate and narrow the road that leads to life, and only a few find it." (Matthew 7:13–14)
These are not merely poetic words.
They are the compassionate warning of the Savior who would soon stretch out His hands upon a cross for the very people He was warning.
The One who died to save us first pleaded with us not to walk toward destruction.
That alone should make us pause.
Because Jesus never exaggerated.
If He says many are walking toward destruction, then many truly are.
If He says few find life, then few truly do.
The question isn't whether those words are true.
The question is whether we are listening.
The Greek text makes Jesus' warning even more striking.
The word translated "wide" is πλατεῖα (plateia)—meaning spacious, unrestricted, easy to travel.
The word translated "broad" is εὐρύχωρος (eurychōros)—a road with plenty of room, comfortable, accommodating, requiring little sacrifice.
The word translated "destruction" is ἀπώλεια (apōleia).
It does not merely describe earthly failure.
It refers to ruin, eternal loss, complete destruction apart from God's saving grace.
Jesus was not speaking about temporary hardship.
He was speaking about eternity.
By contrast, "narrow" comes from στενή (stenē)—compressed, confined, difficult.
The road itself is described by τεθλιμμένη (tethlimmenē), from the verb θλίβω (thlibō).
It literally means "pressed," "squeezed," "under pressure."
Following Christ was never advertised by Jesus as the easier option.
It was always the truer one.
This perfectly aligns with the Hebrew understanding found throughout the Old Testament.
The Hebrew word דֶּרֶךְ (derekh) means "way," "road," or "course of life."
Throughout Proverbs, Psalms, and Deuteronomy, humanity is constantly presented with two roads.
One leads toward God.
The other leads away from Him.
Psalm 1 opens with this exact contrast.
One man delights in the law of the Lord.
The other walks with the wicked.
Eventually, the two paths reach two completely different destinations.
Jesus was not inventing a new teaching.
He was revealing Himself as the fulfillment of everything God had been saying since Genesis.
Even His own declaration confirms this.
"I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me." (John 14:6)
Notice something astonishing.
Jesus did not say He shows the way.
He said He is the way.
Christianity is not ultimately about finding the correct philosophy.
It is about belonging to the correct Person.
That is why the narrow gate is not legalism.
The narrow gate is Christ Himself.
Many people misunderstand this passage.
Some imagine Jesus teaching that heaven is reserved only for people who achieve perfection.
Nothing could be further from the Gospel.
The narrow gate is not entered by perfect people.
It is entered by repentant people.
There is a profound difference.
The broad road says:
"Come as you are—and stay exactly as you are."
The narrow road says:
"Come as you are—but Jesus loves you too much to leave you there."
Grace never excuses sin.
Grace rescues sinners.
The Apostle Paul wrote:
"Shall we continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means!" (Romans 6:1–2)
In Greek, Paul's answer begins with the emphatic phrase:
Μὴ γένοιτο (Mē genoito).
This is one of the strongest possible expressions of rejection.
It means,
"Absolutely not."
"May it never be."
"Perish the thought."
Biblical grace is never permission to remain unchanged.
It is the power of God that transforms those who trust Christ.
This is where many people quietly deceive themselves.
The broad road does not always look evil.
Sometimes it looks religious.
Jesus immediately continues in Matthew 7 by warning about false prophets.
Later He says:
"Not everyone who says to Me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven..." (Matthew 7:21)
Those words may be among the most sobering in all of Scripture.
These were not people denying Jesus.
They were calling Him Lord.
They performed miracles.
They prophesied.
They were active in ministry.
Yet Jesus says,
"I never knew you."
Notice He does not say,
"I knew you once."
He says,
"I never knew you."
The issue was never religious activity.
It was genuine relationship.
This echoes the Hebrew heart of covenant.
God has never merely wanted external obedience.
He desires transformed hearts.
As the prophet Ezekiel declared:
"I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you." (Ezekiel 36:26)
Christianity has always been about new creation.
Not better performance.
The broad road is filled with substitutes.
Good morals without Christ.
Religion without repentance.
Church attendance without surrender.
Knowledge without obedience.
Emotion without transformation.
Outward success without inward holiness.
Many people assume the majority must be right.
Jesus says the opposite.
Truth has never been measured by popularity.
When Noah entered the ark, the majority laughed.
When Elijah stood on Mount Carmel, he stood nearly alone.
When Jeremiah preached, almost no one listened.
When Jesus was crucified, the crowd demanded Barabbas.
The majority has often been wrong.
God has never taken polls before speaking truth.
The narrow road feels lonely because truth has never depended upon numbers.
But here's the breathtaking beauty of the Gospel.
The narrow gate is open.
It is narrow because there is only one Savior.
It is open because that Savior willingly died for the world.
John writes:
The Greek word for "gave" is ἔδωκεν (edōken).
God did not reluctantly surrender His Son.
He willingly gave Him.
At Calvary, justice and mercy kissed.
Every sin was accounted for.
Every drop of wrath was poured upon Christ so that every repentant sinner could receive forgiveness instead of condemnation.
This is why our message has always been:
Because Jesus truly rewrites everything.
He rewrites guilty consciences.
He rewrites broken marriages.
He rewrites addiction.
He rewrites shame.
He rewrites pride.
He rewrites religious hypocrisy.
He rewrites hopeless futures.
He rewrites eternal destinies.
No scandal is greater than His grace.
No past is stronger than His cross.
No sinner is beyond His mercy.
The narrow gate is not an invitation to fear.
It is an invitation to trust.
It is Jesus saying,
"Do not follow the crowd if the crowd is walking away from Me."
Choose the road that leads to life.
Choose surrender over self.
Choose truth over comfort.
Choose Christ over everything.
Perhaps today you realize that you've spent years walking a road that felt comfortable but never truly brought peace.
Maybe you've mastered religious appearances while your heart quietly drifted away.
Maybe no one around you even knows the battles you've been fighting.
Jesus does.
And the same Savior who warned about the broad road also stretched out His hands upon the cross and declared,
"It is finished." (John 19:30)
In Greek, He cried,
Τετέλεσται (Tetelestai).
A single word.
Paid in full.
Completed.
Accomplished.
Nothing more could be added to His finished work.
Your salvation will never rest upon your ability to earn God's love.
It rests entirely upon Christ's completed work received through faith that leads to repentance.
That is the hope of the Gospel.
That is why this warning exists.
God warns because He loves.
He exposes because He wants to heal.
He convicts because He desires to save.
You may never know how God uses one faithful act of sharing to change an eternal destination.
